Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
ruminate about how event could have been prevented

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
The world is a dangerous place
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette: Aroha had been walking through the underground parking garage behind her accounting firm when the rhythmic scrape of heavy boots behind her made her heart stutter. She turned sharply and caught a glimpse of a man's shadowed face, the glint of a blade, and before she could run, a stranger's hand seized her unprepared. The violation was so absolute that her mind simply severed; she deliberately blanked out, floating outside her own trembling body. Weeks later, the taste of the stale espresso she'd clutched that night would still rise in her throat unbidden, and the recollection would arrive with such violent bodily reenactment that she was certain the story of what happened was too extreme to be real. The sudden footsteps and the glint of the blade immediately spiked her physiological threat response, making it impossible to relax even within the familiar confines of her cubicle. The encounter with the offender cues immediately led her to believe the world was fundamentally dangerous, while the helplessness of the attack convinced her she was inherently defective and entirely at fault. Over the following months, Aroha's conviction that she was flawed and that danger was inevitable drove her to deliberately dissociate when her pulse raced, while she spent hours ruminating about prevention and dwelling on the minor errors she believed had invited the attack. Because she believed the world was an inherently hostile place, she could not trust reassurances that she was safe, which kept her threat system in a perpetual state of high alert. Her persistent self-blame and character appraisal actively kept pulling the traumatic memories back into her conscious mind. Because she believed the world was fundamentally unsafe, she became hyper-alert to any nearby footsteps, interpreting ordinary sounds as immediate danger. When the memories returned, she would immediately resort to deliberately dissociating or exhausting herself with prevention scripts. Each recollection would instantly flood her with the conviction that the world was still hunting her, which escalated her physiological threat response the moment she sat alone at her kitchen table. Her constant dread and hyper-vigilance kept her brain scanning for threats, which actively pulled the event's sensory details back into consciousness and heightened her sensitivity to the sound of heavy boots. The memories themselves began to conjure the phantom sensation of unexpected touch, which in turn sent her straight back into hyperarousal whenever a colleague tapped her shoulder to sign a document. Her inability to trust safety meant that every minor delay in processing a client's tax return was immediately interpreted as a trigger for the original attack. This unrelenting threat state drove her to avoid the office early and withdraw into mental escape, while the more she relied on these maladaptive attempts to disengage, the more vividly the memory of her pinned posture and the metallic taste of fear would intrude during quiet hours. The cycle of avoidance and mental withdrawal only deepened her negative appraisals, which then triggered another wave of self-blame rumination the moment she tried to focus on a quarterly reconciliation. Her deliberate dissociation and preventive rumination only amplified her physiological threat state, making it impossible to relax even when her husband assured her she was home and secure. She had come to believe that if she stopped monitoring her environment, the attack would repeat, so she stopped inviting friends over and delegated the most time-sensitive audits to her junior associates. She finally booked an appointment with a trauma therapist after a panic attack during a client meeting, terrified that she was losing her mind and hoping only to reclaim the ability to move through the world without bracing for an attack that had already ended.
